title: Half-Wave
intro: A polarizer throws away whatever is not along its axis. A birefringent plate (retarder) loses nothing: it delays the component along its axis relative to the crossed one, by an amount that grows with the time spent inside it, i.e. with its thickness. A half-wave plate (delay π) mirrors the polarization about its axis. Set the plate's axis and thickness so the horizontal packet arrives vertical, and beat the 25% a lone 45° polarizer would pass.
goal: Place the birefringent plate and set its axis (dial) and thickness (width) so the horizontal packet arrives vertical and passes the vertical guard.

physics.point: A birefringent plate delays one polarization relative to the other and absorbs nothing. At the right thickness, a half-wave plate, it turns horizontal into vertical with no loss.

idea: Split the polarization into a part along the plate's axis and a part across it. Inside the plate the two build up phase at different rates, so one falls behind the other. Nothing is absorbed.

The lag is the retardance Γ. It grows with the time spent inside, so a thicker plate gives a larger lag. At Γ = π, a half-wave plate, the crossed part flips sign, which mirrors the polarization about the plate's axis.
Mirror horizontal about a 45° axis and you get vertical. All of the light can then pass the vertical guard, against 25% for the best single polarizer (at 45°).
At Γ = π/2, a quarter-wave plate, a 45° axis makes the packet circularly polarized, and half of it passes any linear polarizer.
maths: Here the plate builds up phase difference at rate δ = 2 per unit time, and the packet (speed v = 2.5) spends w/v inside a plate of thickness w:

maths.eq:
Γ = δ · w / v = 0.8 · w
half-wave:  w = π / 0.8 ≈ 3.93

maths: For a horizontal input and a plate with axis θ, the share that comes out vertical is:
θ = ±45° and Γ = π give P<sub>V</sub> = 1. A half-wave plate turns linear polarization by 2θ, so θ = 22.5° gives 45° and P<sub>V</sub> = ½.

Measured as a share of the 55% that reaches the target with nothing in the way: 0.96 for w = 3.9 at 45° (P<sub>T</sub> ≈ 53%) and 0.50 for the quarter-wave plate, w ≈ 1.96 (P<sub>T</sub> ≈ 28%). The packet's speeds spread by about 10%, so not all of it sees exactly Γ = π.
try: Set the axis to 45° and the thickness to about 3.9: P<sub>T</sub> ≈ 53%. Thin it to about 2: the packet leaves circular (white in the polarization view) and P<sub>T</sub> halves.
Keep w = 3.9 and turn the axis to 22.5°: the packet leaves at 45° and P<sub>T</sub> ≈ 26%. At 0° or 90° the plate does nothing to a horizontal packet.
Try −45°: it works as well as +45°, because mirroring about either diagonal turns horizontal into vertical.
